​deceased's​ ​own​ ​son,​ ​Milan​ ​Kumar​ ​(Accused​ ​No.​ ​1),​ ​who​ ​hired​ ​Deepak​ ​@​ ​Chauda​ ​(Accused​ ​No.​ ​2)​ ​and​ ​Satyawan​ ​(Accused​ ​No.​ ​3)​ ​to​ ​eliminate​ ​his​ ​father.​ ​3.​ evidence.​ ​103.​ ​The prosecution attempted to build its case on four main pillars:​ ​(i)​ ​motive (property dispute between Milan and his father),​ ​(ii)​ ​disclosure​ ​statements​ ​leading​ ​to​ ​the​ ​recovery​ ​of​ ​the​ ​murder weapon and stolen items,​ ​(iii)​ ​forensic/medical​ ​evidence​ ​matching​ ​the​ ​weapon​ ​to​ ​the​ ​injuries, and​ ​(iv)​ ​electronic​ ​evidence​ ​(Call​ ​Detail​ ​Records)​ ​placing​ ​the​ ​hired accomplices near the crime scene.​ ​104.​ ​To​ ​base​ ​a​ ​conviction​ ​entirely​ ​on​ ​circumstantial​ ​evidence,​ ​the​ ​courts​ ​rely​ ​on​ ​the​ ​"​Panchsheel​​"​ ​or​ ​five​ ​golden​ ​principles​ ​established​ ​by​ ​the​ ​Supreme​ ​Court​ ​in​ ​ Sharad​ ​Birdhichand​ ​Sarda​ ​v.​ ​State​ ​of​ ​Maharashtra​​.​​These​​principles​​mandate​​that​​the​​chain​​of​​circumstances​ ​must​ ​be​ ​fully​ ​established,​ ​must​ ​be​ ​of​ ​a​ ​conclusive​ ​nature,​ ​and​ ​must​ ​unerringly​​point​​only​​towards​​the​​guilt​​of​​the​​accused,​​excluding​​every​ ​other hypothesis.​ ​105.​ ​In​ ​the​ ​present​ ​case,​ ​the​ ​chain​ ​of​ ​circumstances​ ​is​ ​broken​ ​at​ ​multiple critical junctures:​ ​SC No. 7393/2016​ ​Page No.​​40​​/​70​ ​Failure to Establish Motive​ ​106.​ ​In​ ​cases​ ​resting​ ​on​ ​circumstantial​ ​evidence,​ ​the​ ​absence​ ​or​ ​failure​​to​​prove​​motive​​plays​​a​​significant​​role​​and​​favors​​the​​accused.​ ​While​ ​the​ ​prosecution​ ​produced​ ​past​ ​police​ ​complaints​ ​and​ ​a​ ​registered​ ​will​ ​disinheriting​ ​Milan,​ ​the​ ​ocular​ ​testimony​ ​required​ ​to​ ​prove​ ​immediate​ ​motive​ ​and​ ​severe​ ​animosity​ ​collapsed​ ​when​ ​the​ ​family witnesses turned hostile in court.​ ​Complete Collapse of Independent and Family Witnesses​ ​107.​ ​The​​prosecution's​​narrative​​was​​severely​​dented​​because​​almost​ ​all​ ​key​ ​witnesses​ ​turned​ ​hostile.​ ​Family​ ​members,​ ​including​ ​the​ ​deceased's​ ​brother​ ​Balwan​ ​Singh​ ​(PW-10),​ ​daughter​ ​Mukesh​ ​(PW-30),​ ​and​ ​Milan's​ ​wife​ ​Sunita​ ​(PW-27),​ ​denied​ ​or​ ​feigned​ ​ignorance about the property disputes and the alleged confessions.​ ​108.​ ​Crucially,​ ​the​ ​independent​ ​panch​ ​(recovery)​ ​witnesses,​ ​Naresh​ ​(PW-21)​ ​and​ ​Ashok​ ​(PW-29),​ ​who​ ​were​ ​supposed​ ​to​ ​corroborate​​the​ ​physical​ ​recoveries​ ​from​ ​the​ ​accused,​ ​completely​ ​resiled​ ​from​ ​their​ ​police​ ​statements​ ​and​ ​claimed​ ​their​ ​signatures​ ​were​ ​taken​ ​on​ ​blank​ ​papers.​ ​Unreliable and Legally Weak Recoveries​ ​109.​ ​The​​prosecution​​heavily​​relied​​on​​the​​recovery​​of​​the​​knife​​from​ ​a​ ​table​ ​drawer​ ​in​ ​Deepak's​ ​office​ ​and​ ​the​ ​recovery​ ​of​ ​the​​deceased's​ ​mobile​ ​phone,​ ​both​ ​blood​ ​stained,​​and​​bank​​documents​​from​​a​​wheat​ ​container (​​tanki​​) in Satyawan's sister's house.​ ​SC No. 7393/2016​ ​Page No.​​41​​/​70​ ​110.​ ​However,​ ​as​ ​established​ ​by​ ​the​ ​Hon'ble​ ​Supreme​ ​Court​ ​in​ ​the​ ​recent​ ​judgment​ ​ Govind​ ​v.​ ​State​ ​of​ ​Haryana​ ​(2025​ ​INSC​ ​1318)​​,​ ​recoveries​ ​made​ ​from​ ​open​ ​spaces​ ​or​ ​dwelling​ ​houses​ ​accessible​ ​to​ ​other​ ​family​ ​members​ ​or​ ​the​ ​public​ ​cannot​ ​be​ ​solely​ ​relied​ ​upon​ ​to​ ​establish​ ​guilt,​ ​especially​ ​when​​independent​​witnesses​​do​​not​​support​ ​the recovery.​ ​111.​ ​Because​ ​the​ ​recoveries​ ​were​ ​made​ ​from​ ​unlocked/accessible​ ​places​ ​and​ ​the​ ​independent​ ​witnesses​ ​(PW-21​ ​and​ ​PW-29)​ ​turned​ ​hostile,​ ​the​ ​evidentiary​ ​value​ ​of​ ​these​ ​recoveries​ ​is​ ​rendered​ ​highly​ ​suspicious and legally insufficient.​ ​Inconclusive Electronic Evidence (Call Detail Records)​ ​112.​ ​The​ ​prosecution​ ​used​ ​call​ ​detail​ ​records​ ​(CDRs)​ ​to​ ​show​ ​that​ ​the​ ​mobile​ ​phones​ ​of​ ​Deepak​​and​​Satyawan​​were​​active​​on​​the​​Delhi​ ​roaming​ ​network,​ ​with​ ​cell​ ​tower​ ​locations​ ​pointing​ ​to​ ​Masoodpur​ ​(the crime scene) on the night of the murder.​ ​113.​ ​However,​ ​the​ ​Supreme​ ​Court​ ​in​ ​ Rahil​ ​&​ ​Anr.​ ​v.​ ​State​ ​(2025​ ​INSC​ ​858)​ ​explicitly​​held​​that​​cell​​tower​​locations​​merely​​provide​​an​ ​approximate​​area​​corresponding​​to​​the​​operational​​range​​of​​that​​tower,​ ​which​​can​​span​​from​​half​​a​​mile​​to​​two​​miles,​​not​​the​​exact​​site​​of​​the​ ​phone.​ ​The​ ​Court​ ​noted​ ​that​ ​it​ ​is​ ​hazardous​ ​to​ ​rely​ ​solely​ ​on​ ​this​ ​evidence​ ​to​ ​prove​ ​his​ ​presence​ ​at​ ​his​ ​residence​ ​beyond​ ​doubt.​ ​Furthermore,​​the​​Supreme​​Court​​noted​​that​​mere​​telephonic​​exchanges​ ​between​ ​accused​ ​persons​​do​​not​​automatically​​lead​​to​​an​​inference​​of​ ​a criminal conspiracy to murder.​ ​SC No. 7393/2016​ ​Page No.​​42​​/​70​ ​114.​ ​An​ ​analysis​ ​of​ ​the​ ​CDR​ ​break-up​ ​severely​ ​undermines​ ​the​ ​prosecution's​ ​charges​ ​of​ ​criminal​ ​conspiracy​​(Section​​120B​​IPC)​​and​ ​murder​ ​(Section​ ​302​ ​IPC)​ ​against​ ​the​ ​accused,​ ​Milan​ ​(A1),​ ​Deepak​ ​(A2),​ ​and​ ​Satyawan​ ​(A3).​ ​The​ ​prosecution​ ​alleges​ ​that​ ​Milan​ ​hired​ ​Deepak​ ​and​ ​Satyawan​ ​to​​murder​​his​​father,​​Dharam​​Singh.​​However,​ ​the​ ​electronic​ ​evidence​ ​reveals​ ​a​ ​completely​ ​different​ ​narrative​ ​and​ ​highlights fatal flaws in the investigation:​ ​Lack of Communication Between Alleged Conspirators​ ​114.1.​ ​For​​a​​criminal​​conspiracy​​to​​be​​established​​under​​Section​ ​120B,​ ​there​ ​must​ ​be​ ​a​ ​clear​ ​"meeting​ ​of​ ​minds"​ ​or​ ​an​ ​agreement​ ​to​ ​commit​ ​the​ ​illegal​ ​act.​ ​The​ ​CDR​ ​analysis​ ​shows​ ​that​ ​Milan​ ​(09013626162)​ ​had​ ​absolutely​ ​no​ ​contact with Satyawan (09991282094).​ ​114.2.​ ​Furthermore,​ ​Milan​ ​had​ ​only​ ​one​ ​single​ ​phone​ ​call​ ​with​ ​Deepak​ ​(09813176949),​ ​which​ ​lasted​ ​for​ ​a​ ​mere​ ​54​ ​seconds​ ​on​ ​03.10.2011,​ ​nearly​ ​two​ ​months​ ​before​ ​the​ ​murder​​on​​26/27.11.2011.​​This​​single,​​brief​​interaction​​is​ ​highly​ ​insufficient​ ​to​ ​establish​ ​an​ ​elaborate​ ​murder​ ​conspiracy.​ ​The Unexplained Role of Krishan S/o Naresh​ ​114.3.​ ​The​ ​CDR​ ​analysis​ ​exposes​ ​a​ ​glaring​ ​loophole​ ​in​ ​the​ ​prosecution's​ ​case​ ​by​ ​revealing​ ​Krishan​ ​S/o​ ​Naresh​ ​(09813214030)​ ​as​ ​a​ ​central,​ ​highly​ ​active​ ​node​ ​of​ ​communication​ ​who​ ​was​ ​completely​ ​ignored​ ​by​ ​the​ ​prosecution.​ ​SC No. 7393/2016​ ​Page No.​​43​​/​70​ ​114.4.​ ​Krishan​ ​and​ ​the​ ​Deceased​​:​ ​Krishan​ ​had​ ​extensive​ ​communication​ ​with​ ​the​ ​deceased,​ ​Dharam​ ​Singh​ ​(09312340075),​ ​exchanging​ ​26​ ​calls​ ​(21​ ​outgoing,​ ​05​ ​incoming)​​and​​4​​SMS​​messages​​between​​01.10.2011​​and​ ​29.10.2011.​ ​114.5.​ ​Krishan​ ​and​ ​the​ ​Alleged​ ​Hitman​​:​ ​Simultaneously,​ ​Krishan​ ​was​ ​in​ ​heavy​ ​contact​ ​with​ ​the​ ​co-accused​ ​Deepak,​ ​exchanging​ ​44​​calls​​(16​​incoming,​​28​​outgoing)​ ​and 1 SMS. He also had contact with Satyawan.​ ​No Contact Between Deceased and Accused​ ​114.6.​ ​The​​CDRs​​confirm​​that​​the​​deceased,​​Dharam​​Singh,​​had​ ​absolutely​​no​​phone​​calls​​or​​SMS​​exchanges​​with​​his​​son​ ​Milan​ ​(A1),​ ​or​ ​the​ ​alleged​ ​hitmen​ ​Deepak​ ​(A2)​ ​and​ ​Satyawan (A3).​ ​115.​ ​The​ ​CDR​ ​analysis​ ​also​ ​shatters​ ​this​ ​chain​ ​of​ ​circumstances​ ​in​ ​the following ways:​ ​Failure to Prove Conspiracy (Section 120B IPC)​ ​115.1.​ ​The​ ​prosecution​ ​cannot​ ​prove​ ​a​ ​conspiracy​ ​between​ ​Milan,​ ​Deepak,​ ​and​ ​Satyawan​ ​when​ ​the​ ​electronic​ ​evidence​ ​shows​ ​almost​ ​zero​ ​communication​ ​between​ ​them​ ​leading​ ​up​ ​to​ ​the​ ​crime.​ ​As​ ​the​ ​Supreme​ ​Court​ ​noted​ ​in​ ​Rahil​ ​&​ ​Anr.​ ​v.​ ​State​ ​(2025​ ​INSC​ ​858)​​,​ ​mere​ ​telephonic​ ​exchanges​ ​do​ ​not​ ​automatically​ ​lead​ ​to​ ​an​ ​inference​ ​of​ ​a​ ​conspiracy​ ​to​ ​murder;​ ​therefore,​ ​a​ ​lack​ ​of​ ​SC No. 7393/2016​ ​Page No.​​44​​/​70​ ​telephonic​ ​exchanges​ ​between​ ​the​ ​alleged​ ​mastermind​ ​and​ ​the​ ​hitmen​ ​makes​ ​the​ ​conspiracy​ ​theory​ ​virtually​ ​impossible to sustain.​ ​Alternative Hypothesis Exists​ ​115.2.​ ​Circumstantial​​evidence​​must​​unerringly​​point​​only​​to​​the​ ​guilt​ ​of​ ​the​ ​accused.​ ​The​ ​CDRs​ ​actively​ ​introduce​ ​a​ ​highly​ ​plausible​ ​alternative​ ​hypothesis​ ​that​ ​Krishan​ ​S/o​ ​Naresh,​​who​​was​​in​​constant,​​heavy​​communication​​with​ ​both​ ​the​ ​victim​ ​and​ ​the​ ​alleged​ ​hitman​ ​(Deepak),​ ​was​ ​deeply​ ​involved​ ​in​​the​​events​​leading​​to​​Dharam​​Singh's​ ​death.​ ​Because​ ​the​ ​prosecution​ ​did​ ​not​ ​investigate​ ​Krishan, they failed to rule out this alternative hypothesis.​ ​Missing Links Create Reasonable Doubt​ ​115.3.​ ​The​ ​Supreme​ ​Court​ ​has​ ​held​ ​that​ ​if​ ​an​ ​iota​ ​of​ ​doubt​ ​creeps​ ​in​ ​at​ ​any​ ​stage​ ​in​ ​the​ ​sequence​ ​of​ ​events,​ ​or​ ​if​ ​there​ ​is​ ​a​ ​missing​ ​link,​ ​a​ ​finding​ ​of​ ​guilt​ ​cannot​ ​be​ ​recorded,​ ​and​ ​the​ ​benefit​ ​of​ ​the​ ​doubt​ ​must​ ​flow​ ​to​ ​the​ ​accused.​ ​The​ ​stark​ ​contradiction​ ​between​ ​the​ ​prosecution's​ ​theory​ ​of​ ​Milan​ ​as​​the​​mastermind​​and​​the​ ​objective​ ​electronic​ ​data​ ​showing​ ​Milan's​ ​isolation​​from​ ​the co-accused creates an insurmountable missing link.​ ​116.​ ​The​ ​CDR​ ​data​ ​suggests​ ​that​ ​Krishan​ ​S/o​ ​Naresh​ ​was​ ​the​ ​primary​ ​connecting​ ​link​ ​between​ ​the​ ​deceased​ ​and​ ​the​ ​alleged​ ​accomplices.​ ​The​ ​prosecution's​ ​failure​ ​to​ ​investigate​ ​Krishan,​ ​array​ ​SC No. 7393/2016​ ​Page No.​​45​​/​70​ ​him​ ​as​ ​an​ ​accused,​ ​or​ ​explain​ ​his​​extensive​​communications​​leaves​​a​ ​massive, unexplained gap in the narrative.​ ​Conclusion​ ​117.​ ​The​ ​objective​ ​electronic​ ​evidence​ ​directly​ ​contradicts​ ​the​ ​prosecution's​ ​theory​ ​of​ ​a​ ​coordinated​ ​conspiracy​ ​led​ ​by​ ​Milan​ ​(A1).​ ​Instead​​of​​proving​​guilt,​​the​​CDR​​analysis​​highlights​​a​​fundamentally​ ​flawed​​investigation​​that​​ignored​​the​​most​​active​​communicating​​party​ ​(Krishan).​​Consequently,​​the​​chain​​of​​circumstances​​is​​broken,​​and​​the​ ​charges​ ​under​ ​Section​ ​120B​ ​and​ ​Section​ ​302​ ​IPC​ ​remain​ ​unproved​ ​beyond a reasonable doubt.​ ​118.​ ​When​ ​a​ ​case​ ​rests​ ​on​ ​circumstantial​ ​evidence,​ ​suspicion,​ ​no​ ​matter​ ​how​ ​grave,​ ​cannot​ ​substitute​ ​legal​ ​proof.​ ​The​ ​prosecution​ ​has​ ​failed​ ​to​ ​conclusively​ ​link​ ​the​ ​accused​ ​to​ ​the​ ​crime​ ​scene​ ​through​ ​unassailable​ ​physical​ ​evidence,​ ​and​ ​the​ ​reliance​ ​on​ ​cell-tower​ ​triangulation​ ​and​ ​recoveries​ ​from​ ​accessible​ ​places​ ​falls​ ​short​ ​of​ ​the​ ​stringent​ ​legal​ ​standards​ ​required​ ​for​ ​a​ ​conviction.​ ​Therefore,​ ​the​ ​accused​ ​persons​ ​are​ ​entitled​ ​to​ ​the​ ​benefit​ ​of​ ​the​ ​doubt,​ ​meaning​​the​ ​charges under Section 120B and Section 302 IPC remain unproved.​ ​119.​ ​The​ ​Court​ ​finds​ ​that​ ​the​ ​prosecution​ ​has​ ​miserably​ ​failed​ ​to​ ​prove​ ​the​ ​guilt​ ​of​ ​the​ ​accused​ ​persons​ ​beyond​ ​a​ ​reasonable​​doubt​​on​ ​both charges.​ D​ ecision​ ​120.​ ​In​ ​view​ ​of​ ​the​ ​above​ ​observations​ ​and​ ​findings,​ ​the​ ​final​ ​decision of the Court
